review_note: Figures sourced from OECD Health at a Glance 2025 (published Nov 2025) and Eurostat 2024 data (published 2025). Re-verify against primary sources at least annually — these are the kind of numbers that change with each annual release.

indicators.value: 100% of the population is covered for a core set of services in Greece
indicators.source: OECD Health at a Glance 2025, Greece country note

indicators.value: 27% of people in Greece report satisfaction with the availability of quality healthcare
indicators.source: OECD Health at a Glance 2025, Greece country note

indicators.value: 61% of health spending in Greece is covered by mandatory prepayment (public/social schemes)
indicators.source: OECD Health at a Glance 2025, Greece country note

indicators.value: 12.1% of people in Greece report unmet healthcare needs due to cost, distance or waiting times
indicators.denominator_note: Denominator: the whole population aged 16+, regardless of whether they reported needing care. Do not merge this figure with unmet_needs_eu_profile below — they measure different populations and are not directly comparable.

indicators.value: 21.9% — the highest share in the EU — of people in Greece who reported needing medical care said they could not get it
indicators.comparator: EU average by this same measure is 3.6%
indicators.source: Eurostat, 2024 data (hlth_silc_08b), as cited in the EU State of Health / Country Health Profile 2025 series
indicators.denominator_note: Denominator: ONLY people who reported actually needing medical or dental care in the past 12 months. This is why the figure is much higher than unmet_needs_oecd above — narrower, more affected population.

indicators.value: Households in Greece cover more than one third of total health spending directly out of pocket
indicators.comparator: among the highest shares in the OECD, alongside Mexico, Chile and Latvia
indicators.caveat: This measures direct household payment share of total health expenditure. It does NOT by itself prove people were uninsured, nor that a private contract rejected a claim — it includes co-payments, medicines, services outside any benefit package, and discretionary private choice of doctor/hospital.

argument_translations.reads_as: A meaningful share of the population faces real barriers to getting care when they need it — this is a description of access barriers, not a claim that private insurance eliminates them entirely.
A material part of healthcare in Greece is financed directly by households rather than pooled cover — insurance can improve financial predictability for the portion of spending it actually covers.

Availability of quality care, as experienced by residents, falls well short of what people in most other OECD countries report — this supports discussing alternative access routes, not disparaging the system.
